newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian rouble move shows inflation confidence.
newsitem.headline: Russian rouble move shows inflation confidence.

text.p: Russia's plans to lop three zeroes off its bloated rouble next year, crowning six years of tough economic reforms, signal confidence that soaring prices and a tumbling rouble are history, economists said on Monday.

The main impact of the move will be psychological -- it will break the cycle of inflationary expectations which led ordinary Russians to shun the ever-depreciating rouble -- and make life easier for ordinary people and companies.
It will also signal a return to normality in everyday life after the upheaval of the break-up of the Soviet Union and start of market reforms in Russia.
From January 1, 1998, one new rouble will equal 1,000 old ones, or 17 cents in current rates.

In contrast to Soviet-era currency reforms, which amounted to a sudden and unexpected confiscation of money to reduce demand in the shortage-ridden economy, the new and old roubles will circulate together for one year, and the central bank will exchange old roubles for four more years to the end of 2002.

"It signals confidence in the central bank and government that they're going to be able to hold inflation in the coming years to below 10 percent," said Charles Blitzer, chief economist, emerging markets, at U.S. investment bank Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette.
"It's psychological and convenient rather than economic. There's no change in monetary policy."
Central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin stressed continuity, saying currency targets for this year remain in force.
"I don't see any reason for a dramatic change in currency policy for 1998. The gradual devaluation of the rouble will most likely continue in line with inflation," he said.

This was the view of Russian markets too. The rouble was barely changed at about 5,800 per dollar after dipping for a few minutes in early trading in a knee-jerk reaction, on fears the redenomination could prompt a flight from roubles.
But the terms of the swap quickly brought the rouble back again.
In fact the rouble has been appreciating in real terms recently and Dubinin hinted that this would continue.
"We hope the new heavy, firm rouble will firm in the future and its inflationary depreciation will slow down even more than this year," he said.

But by allowing the rouble to devalue roughly in line with inflation rather than pegging it to another currency, Russia is not risking the sort of speculative attack suffered recently by the Czech Republic and other emerging markets, said Christopher Granville, director of research at United City Bank.
The International Monetary Fund's representative in Moscow, Martin Gilman, said the move was a sign of Russia's growing economic maturity.
"It's certainly an encouraging sign of the government's confidence in its ability to maintain low inflation," he said.
"It's more symbolic. In terms of economic fundamentals it doesn't change anything," he said.
But some analysts were mildly surprised at the timing of the move, which Dubinin said had been agreed on in August last year.
"Normally you would expect a longer track record on inflation. The timing is quite aggressive," said Granville.
Inflation has slowed sharply over the last couple of years from year-on-year rates of over 1,000 percent in 1993 in the early stages of Russia's market reforms.

The year-on-year rate in June was 14.5 percent and, apart from January this year when a number of government-imposed price rises took effect, the monthly rate has been below two percent since early 1996. The rate for July is likely to be 0.9 percent.

If Russians start to stockpile goods, inflation could pick up this month, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said. The rate for the whole of 1997 would probably be a little above the government's forecast 11.8 percent, he said.
Announcing the redenomination, President Boris Yeltsin said, however, that the aim was to make the rouble respected at home and throughout the world again.
In terms of psychological impact, that would make it logical to broaden the convertibility of the rouble and allow it to be traded at airports and banks outside Russia, Granville said.
The redenomination starts on January 1, 1998, the same day as Russia removes remaining barriers to non-resident investment in its government securities market, he noted.

But Gilman of the IMF thought Russia was unlikely to remove capital controls fully, and the coincidence of the T-bill market liberalisation and rouble redenomination just reflected the fact that reforms are progressing on several fronts simultaneously.
Putting the rouble on a par with other currencies could also clear the way for a rouble Eurobond, said Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Russian investment bank Troika Dialog.
"There are going to be rouble instruments in the market. It's just a question of when exactly. My guess is we'll see something next year," he said.
